content: This lower representation highlights the barriers to entry in the structural steel sector, where the high costs of fabrication equipment, skilled labor, and raw materials make it difficult for emerging micro-enterprises to compete for formal contracts. The remaining market share is naturally occupied by the highest tier (Grades 7 to 9), which handles large-scale, high-value infrastructure and heavy industrial projects requiring massive capital and advanced engineering capabilities. The operational relevance of CIDB grading is inextricably linked to the rigorous material and structural standards governing the South African steel industry. While CIDB grades assess contractor capacity, the actual execution of fabrication projects must adhere strictly to technical specifications. As of June 2026, structural steel grading requirements remain a critical topic influenced by both national standards and evolving industry practices. The Southern African Institute of Steel Construction (SAISC) is regarded as a key authority on industry standards within the region. Recently, the SAISC released its 2026 Rondo Trade Product Guide, which purportedly covers essential technical topics such as steel grades, section types, and structural standards [43] . Although specific grading requirements are highly detailed within such proprietary guides, they serve as a comprehensive and current resource for professionals operating within the South African market [43] . The introduction of new import duties on May 15, 2026, as revised by the International Trade Administration Commission (ITAC), is expected to indirectly impact the steel market by affecting material costs and availability [41] . While this policy does not explicitly address grading specifications relevant to construction projects, the resulting fluctuations in material costs can heavily influence a contractor's financial stability and, consequently, their CIDB grading status [41] . Contractors in lower CIDB grades (Grades 1 to 3) may find themselves particularly vulnerable to sudden increases in the cost of raw materials, further explaining their lower 20.0% representation in successful contractor selections. As trade policies and material costs continue to evolve, the CIDB grading system will remain a vital barometer of contractor resilience and capability in the dynamic South African engineering and maintenance sector.
